chapters.1: While living among Jewish exiles in Babylon, Ezekiel sees an overwhelming vision of God's glory: four strange living creatures with multiple faces and wings, moving wheels full of eyes, and above it all a throne with a figure radiant like fire. Overwhelmed, Ezekiel falls on his face before this vision of God's majesty.
chapters.2: God commissions Ezekiel as a prophet to the rebellious people of Israel, warning him they will likely refuse to listen but telling him to speak anyway. In a symbolic act, Ezekiel is given a scroll filled with words of judgment and mourning to "eat."
chapters.3: Ezekiel eats the scroll, which tastes sweet like honey even though its message is one of judgment. God appoints him as a "watchman" responsible for warning Israel of danger, and he is temporarily made silent and confined until God gives him specific words to speak.
chapters.4: God has Ezekiel act out the coming siege of Jerusalem using a model city, by lying bound on his side for a set number of days representing the years of Israel's and Judah's sin, and by eating meager rationed food and water to symbolize the famine conditions coming during the siege.
chapters.5: Ezekiel shaves his hair and divides it into portions representing how the people of Jerusalem will die by sword, famine, and scattering because of their persistent sin. God declares that Jerusalem's punishment will be so severe it will shock the surrounding nations.
chapters.6: God pronounces judgment against the mountains and hills of Israel where the people practiced idol worship, promising to destroy their altars and high places along with the people who worshiped there. Yet he also promises to preserve a remnant who will remember him in exile and feel genuine remorse.
chapters.7: Ezekiel announces that "the end" has come for Israel, describing in intense language a day of inescapable disaster where wealth, violence, and corrupt leadership will all collapse together. Even silver and gold will become worthless since they could not buy anyone's safety from God's judgment.
chapters.8: In a vision, Ezekiel is transported to the Jerusalem temple and shown a series of escalating idolatrous practices happening there in secret, including elders burning incense to idols, women mourning for a foreign god, and men worshiping the sun with their backs to God's temple. God declares these outrages are why he will show no mercy.
chapters.9: God sends executioners through Jerusalem to kill those practicing these abominations, sparing only those marked with a special sign for mourning the city's sin. Ezekiel pleads for mercy on the remnant, but God insists judgment is deserved because of the city's great wickedness.
chapters.10: Ezekiel again sees the cherubim and the wheels from his earlier vision, and watches as the glory of the Lord departs from the temple's threshold and moves toward the cherubim, symbolically preparing to leave Jerusalem altogether because of its corruption.
chapters.11: Ezekiel confronts corrupt leaders plotting evil in the city, and one of them, Pelatiah, dies as Ezekiel is speaking. God promises that although Israel will be scattered among the nations, he will eventually gather them back, give them new hearts, and restore them as his people; the chapter ends with the glory of the Lord departing from the city entirely.
chapters.12: Ezekiel acts out the coming exile by packing his belongings and digging through a wall to escape in front of the watching people, representing how Jerusalem's leader will try to flee the city's fall but be captured. God rebukes the people's belief that disaster is always far off, insisting that the fulfillment of these warnings is near.
chapters.13: God condemns false prophets who claim to speak for him but only make up comforting messages from their own imagination, like people patching a crumbling wall with weak plaster. He also condemns women practicing manipulative divination, promising to expose and stop both groups.
chapters.14: God tells Ezekiel that people who come to inquire of him while secretly clinging to idols in their hearts will not receive a true answer. He also states that even if righteous figures like Noah, Daniel, and Job were present, they could only save themselves, not the whole sinful nation, from the coming judgment, though a remnant will still survive to witness it.
chapters.15: God compares Jerusalem to a worthless vine branch, useful for nothing even when healthy and even less useful once burned by fire. The point is that the city has no special value left to shield it from the destruction it has brought on itself.
chapters.16: Using an extended, graphic allegory, God describes Jerusalem as an abandoned baby he rescued, raised, and married, lavishing her with beauty and riches, only for her to become unfaithful by worshiping idols and even sacrificing her own children. Despite pronouncing severe judgment for this betrayal, God ends by promising to remember his covenant and ultimately restore the relationship.
chapters.17: Ezekiel tells a riddle-like parable about two eagles and a vine, representing how King Zedekiah of Judah broke his covenant with Babylon by seeking help from Egypt instead, which God says will lead to his downfall. The chapter ends with a promise that God himself will eventually plant a new, flourishing cedar on Israel's mountain, symbolizing future restoration.
chapters.18: God rejects the proverb blaming children for their parents' sins, insisting that each person is responsible for their own choices: the righteous will live and the wicked will die based on their own conduct, not their ancestors'. He stresses that anyone, righteous or wicked, can change course, and pleads with Israel to turn from sin and live, since he takes no pleasure in anyone's death.
chapters.19: Ezekiel sings a lament comparing Judah's recent kings to young lions raised by a lioness, both of whom were eventually captured and led away in chains to foreign lands. He also compares the nation to a once-flourishing vine now uprooted and planted in a dry, barren wilderness.
chapters.20: When elders come to consult Ezekiel, God recounts Israel's long history of rebellion, from idolatry in Egypt through repeated disobedience in the wilderness and in the land, despite his continued mercy. He insists he will still ultimately gather and purify his scattered people for his own name's sake, even while still having to act in judgment now.
chapters.21: God declares that his "sword" of judgment is drawn and sharpened against Jerusalem and will strike without turning back. The chapter also describes the king of Babylon using divination to decide to attack Jerusalem, and pronounces a related judgment against the Ammonites who gloated over Judah's troubles.
chapters.22: God calls Jerusalem a "bloody city" guilty of murder, idolatry, oppression of the vulnerable, and sexual immorality, with corrupt officials, priests, and prophets all contributing to its corruption. He compares the people to impure metal he must melt down in judgment, and laments that no one stepped up to intercede and prevent the coming disaster.
chapters.23: Using the allegory of two unfaithful sisters, Samaria (Aholah) and Jerusalem (Aholibah), Ezekiel describes how both kingdoms "prostituted" themselves to foreign powers and their idols, with Jerusalem becoming even more corrupt than Samaria had been before its destruction. Because of this, God declares that Jerusalem will suffer a similarly severe judgment at the hands of the very nations she courted.
chapters.24: Ezekiel acts out a parable of a boiling pot full of meat and bones representing Jerusalem, a city so corrupted by bloodshed that it cannot be cleansed, as the Babylonian siege begins. In a deeply personal sign, Ezekiel's own wife dies suddenly and he is told not to publicly mourn her, modeling how the people will be too shocked and devastated by the coming destruction of the temple and their families to even properly grieve.
chapters.25: God pronounces judgment on four nations that mistreated or mocked Judah in its downfall: Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines. Each is condemned for gloating over or taking revenge against Judah's suffering, and each will be destroyed or handed over to other peoples as a result.
chapters.26: God announces judgment against the wealthy trading city of Tyre for rejoicing over Jerusalem's fall, predicting that King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon will besiege and demolish it. Tyre's great walls and towers will be reduced to a bare rock, and its noise and music will be silenced forever.
chapters.27: Ezekiel sings an extended lament over Tyre as a magnificent trading ship, cataloging the many nations that supplied its fine materials and goods. The lament pictures this impressive vessel ultimately wrecked at sea, with sailors and merchants mourning its sudden, total loss.
chapters.28: God condemns the arrogant ruler of Tyre for claiming to be a god because of his wisdom and wealth, declaring he will instead die like any mortal at the hands of invaders. In a related poetic lament describing a glorious, bejeweled figure who fell from a holy place through pride and corruption, God also pronounces judgment on the neighboring city of Sidon, while promising future safety for Israel once its enemies are dealt with.
chapters.29: God turns his judgment toward Egypt and Pharaoh, comparing him to a great river monster who claims the Nile as his own creation. He predicts Egypt will become desolate and scattered for forty years, after which it will be restored but only as a weak, minor kingdom, no longer a false source of confidence for Israel.
chapters.30: Ezekiel describes a coming "day of the Lord" striking Egypt and its allied nations with the sword, as Babylon's king destroys its cities, idols, and leadership. Egypt's strength and pride will be completely broken.
chapters.31: God compares Egypt's Pharaoh to a magnificent, towering cedar tree (illustrated by the earlier example of Assyria) that grew proud in its greatness, only to be cut down and cast into the realm of the dead. The lesson is that no nation's height or glory can protect it from judgment when it becomes arrogant.
chapters.32: Ezekiel sings a funeral lament over Pharaoh and Egypt, picturing their downfall as a great sea creature caught in a net and consumed, with darkness covering the land. The chapter closes with a grim vision of Egypt joining other once-mighty, now-fallen nations like Assyria, Elam, and Edom in the realm of the dead, all humiliated together.
chapters.33: God reaffirms Ezekiel's role as a "watchman" responsible for warning people of danger, explaining that each person's own choices, not their past, determine whether they live or die spiritually. News arrives that Jerusalem has fallen, after which Ezekiel's message shifts from warning of judgment to the possibility of a genuinely changed life, though he notes the people still hear his words without truly acting on them.
chapters.34: God condemns Israel's corrupt "shepherds" (its leaders) for exploiting the people instead of caring for them, leaving the flock scattered and vulnerable. He promises to personally gather and shepherd his scattered people himself, and to set up a future shepherd like David to care for them under a covenant of peace and safety.
chapters.35: God pronounces judgment against Mount Seir (Edom) for its lasting hostility toward Israel and for gloating over Israel's downfall and seizing its land. Because of this hatred and violence, Edom itself will become a desolate wasteland.
chapters.36: God promises to restore the mountains and land of Israel, which have been mocked and plundered by surrounding nations, making them fruitful and inhabited again. He also promises to cleanse the people spiritually, giving them a new heart and a new spirit so they can genuinely follow him, not because they deserve it but for the sake of his own reputation.
chapters.37: In the famous vision of the valley of dry bones, Ezekiel sees a vast number of bones come back to life as God breathes into them, symbolizing Israel's national revival after being as good as dead in exile. God also has Ezekiel join two sticks into one, representing the eventual reunification of Israel and Judah under a single future ruler like David, in a lasting covenant of peace.
chapters.38: God announces a future invasion of Israel by a coalition of nations led by a figure named Gog, from the land of Magog, who will attack Israel's seemingly peaceful, unwalled communities. God declares that he himself will intervene dramatically with earthquakes, plague, and storms to defeat this invading force and reveal his power to the nations.
chapters.39: God continues describing the total defeat of Gog's invading army, which will be destroyed on the mountains of Israel and left as food for birds and animals. Afterward, Israel will spend months collecting weapons and burying the dead to cleanse the land, after which God promises to fully restore his people and pour out his Spirit on them.
chapters.40: In a detailed vision, Ezekiel is led by a heavenly guide who measures a magnificent future temple complex, starting with its outer wall, gates, and courts. The precise measurements and structure emphasize the order, holiness, and grandeur of this ideal temple compared to the one destroyed earlier.
chapters.41: The vision continues as the guide measures the interior of the temple itself, including the main sanctuary, the inner sanctuary (holy of holies), and surrounding side chambers. Decorative carvings of cherubim and palm trees are also described throughout the structure.
chapters.42: Ezekiel's guide measures the priests' chambers surrounding the temple, used for eating holy offerings and changing garments, and then measures the overall dimensions of the whole temple complex. The detailed layout underscores a clear separation between what is holy and what is common.
chapters.43: The glory of the Lord dramatically returns to fill this new temple, arriving from the east just as Ezekiel had earlier seen it depart. God declares he will dwell there permanently if the people abandon their idolatry, and gives instructions for consecrating the temple's altar through a seven-day ritual.
chapters.44: God decrees that the east gate through which his glory entered will remain permanently shut, reserved symbolically for him and the prince. He also sets stricter rules for temple service, excluding unfaithful Levites from full priestly duties while reserving the priesthood for the faithful descendants of Zadok, who must follow special purity standards.
chapters.45: God sets aside a holy portion of land for the sanctuary, the priests, the Levites, and the city, along with a portion for the prince, so no one encroaches on what belongs to God or exploits the people. He also establishes fair standards of measurement and lays out offerings the prince must provide for various feasts and sacrifices throughout the year.
chapters.46: This chapter details worship practices for the restored temple, including how the prince and the people are to enter for sabbaths and festivals, and regulations for various offerings. It also addresses property rules, ensuring the prince cannot permanently seize land from the people for his own family's gain.
chapters.47: Ezekiel sees a river flowing out from under the temple, growing from a trickle into a deep, life-giving river that heals the sea and causes abundant trees and fish to flourish wherever it flows. The chapter also marks out the future boundaries of the land to be divided among the twelve tribes of Israel.
chapters.48: The book closes by assigning specific portions of the restored land to each of the twelve tribes, along with special allotments for the priests, the Levites, the city, and the prince. The vision ends with the city gates named after the tribes and the city itself renamed "The LORD is there," symbolizing God's permanent presence among his people.
